summary: Defines a CGI interface for SIP, letting scripts on a SIP server provide services by handling requests, much as web CGI scripts do for web servers. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Web servers can run little helper scripts to answer you. This lets internet phone servers run helper scripts too.

questions: how to write scripts for a sip server
subtitle: A scripting interface for building telephony services on SIP servers.

tldr.problem: SIP servers need a way for developers to create and deploy custom telephony services like call forwarding or voicemail. Traditional server-side mechanisms like CGI have worked well for HTTP, but SIP requires different operations like proxying and forking.
tldr.mechanism: SIP CGI defines a gateway interface adapted from HTTP CGI, allowing scripts to run on SIP servers. Scripts receive request information via environment variables and invoke actions by outputting special directives, allowing them to proxy requests, forward responses, and maintain state across multiple messages.
tldr.outcome: Developers can use familiar scripting languages and tools to build SIP services, bringing rapid service development practices from the web to Internet telephony.

facts.label: Supported programming languages
facts.value: Perl, C, VisualBasic, TCL, and any language with environment variable access

today: RFC 3050 is an Informational specification published in January 2001. It defines one approach to rapid service creation for SIP networks. While SIP CGI remains informational rather than a standard, the concepts influenced service creation environments in commercial SIP deployments. Other service creation approaches like SIP servlet containers and server-embedded scripting also became common.

sections.title: Scripting for Telephony Services
sections.content:
The Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) enables Internet telephony by signaling the setup and teardown of multimedia sessions. While SIP defines the basic protocol, real-world telephony services—such as call forwarding, voicemail, and conference bridging—require service-specific logic. The question is: how can developers rapidly create and deploy these services?

In the web world, the Common Gateway Interface (CGI) provides an answer. Web servers execute scripts that generate dynamic content in response to HTTP requests. Developers can write scripts in Perl, C, JavaScript, or other languages, and the scripts have direct access to all request information and full control over the response. CGI has proven popular because it is language-independent, exposes all headers, and allows full control over response generation.

SIP services could benefit from a similar mechanism. However, SIP differs from HTTP in important ways. A SIP proxy may fork a request to multiple downstream servers. A script may need to maintain control across multiple message exchanges (requests and responses). SIP emphasizes header information more than HTTP does. These differences mean SIP CGI must extend the HTTP CGI model.
sections.eli5: When you visit a web page, the server runs a script that builds the page. Phone servers could work the same way: run a script when a call comes in, and the script decides where to send it.

sections.title: How SIP CGI Works
sections.content:
A SIP server runs CGI scripts when messages arrive. For each message, the server sets environment variables containing metadata about the message: the sender, recipient, request URI, SIP headers, and so on. The script reads stdin to get the message body. When the script completes, it writes output to stdout specifying actions the server should take.

Scripts output action lines that tell the server what to do. For example, to generate a response, a script outputs SIP/2.0 200 OK. To proxy a request to a URI, the script outputs CGI-PROXY-REQUEST sip:user@example.com SIP/2.0. Scripts can output multiple actions and accompanying SIP headers. Following the action line, a blank line and optional message body complete the message.

A crucial innovation for SIP CGI is state maintenance. In HTTP, a CGI script runs once per request and terminates. In SIP, a single incoming request can generate multiple outgoing requests, each with its own responses. A script may need to process these responses and make further decisions. SIP CGI allows a script to return an opaque cookie to the server. When the server invokes the script again for the same transaction, it passes the cookie back, allowing the script to maintain state without server-side databases.
sections.eli5: A phone server calls a script when a call arrives. The script reads what the call is about, decides what to do, and writes commands telling the server to forward the call, play a message, or hang up. The script can ask the server to call it again later with a special token so it remembers what it was doing.

sections.title: Key Differences from HTTP CGI
sections.content:
While SIP CGI is based on HTTP CGI, several important differences reflect SIP's unique requirements. In HTTP, only the origin server runs CGI scripts. In SIP, both proxy servers and registrars execute scripts. SIP servers perform four fundamental operations: proxying requests to other servers, returning responses from other servers, generating new requests, and generating responses locally. HTTP servers focus almost entirely on generating responses.

HTTP CGI scripts run once per transaction. SIP CGI scripts may run multiple times. A script can output a CGI-AGAIN yes action to indicate it wants to be invoked again when the next message arrives. This allows a script to apply custom logic to responses from proxied requests or to handle ACK and CANCEL messages. For example, a call-forwarding script might proxy the initial request to the primary destination. When that fails, the server invokes the script again with the failure response. The script then proxies the request to a backup destination.

SIP headers carry much more protocol semantics than HTTP headers. Therefore, SIP CGI scripts need access to all headers, not just a few. The specification recommends that servers provide all non-sensitive headers to scripts as environment variables with the prefix SIP_.
sections.eli5: Phone networks are more complicated than web servers. A script might need to fork a call to multiple numbers and decide what to do based on which one answers. So phone scripts can be called multiple times for one call.

sections.title: Script Execution and Actions
sections.content:
When a new request arrives at a SIP server, the server invokes a CGI script by executing it (or linking it as a subroutine). The server passes the request metadata via environment variables and the request body via stdin. The script executes, reads this information, and writes output to stdout.

The script output contains one or more messages, each consisting of an action line, optional CGI headers (starting with CGI-), optional SIP headers, a blank line, and an optional message body. Action lines include Status (to generate a response), CGI-PROXY-REQUEST (to forward a request), CGI-FORWARD-RESPONSE (to forward a previously received response), CGI-SET-COOKIE (to save state), and CGI-AGAIN (to request reinvocation on the next message).

The CGI-REQUEST-TOKEN header allows a script to label outgoing requests so responses can be matched back. This is essential for forking: when a script proxies to multiple destinations, responses arrive without inherent correlation to the request branch. By placing a unique token in each request, the script can later identify which response came from which branch.
sections.eli5: The script reads information about the call, makes decisions, and outputs commands. Commands can say 'send a response', 'forward this to another number', 'remember this information' or 'call me again when the next thing happens'.

sections.title: Security and Implementation
sections.content:
CGI scripts execute with significant privileges. A script can generate arbitrary SIP transactions, spoof responses, and directly access the server. Administrators must treat CGI scripts as security-sensitive as the SIP server itself and perform equivalent security review before installation.

Scripts must be careful with authentication. Adding or removing SIP headers can break authentication if those headers are below the Authorization header in the received message. For encrypted SIP messages, the encrypted portion arrives in the message body, and scripts should not modify it in ways that invalidate encryption.

Sensitive header fields (like Authorization headers containing credentials) should not be passed to scripts unless explicitly configured. Data length considerations also matter: scripts should not assume that fixed-size buffers can hold entire request bodies. Some implementations define timeouts, maximum request limits, or other resource constraints on script execution.

The specification defines system-specific details for Unix and Microsoft Windows platforms, including environment variable mechanisms and character set handling.
sections.eli5: Scripts are very powerful, so only trusted scripts should be installed. Scripts need to be careful not to break security features or modify encrypted messages.
